title: Making plots with ggplot2: Barplots and Scatterplots
text:
ggplot2 is a package built within the tidyverse package for creating awesome graphs!
library(tidyverse)
#Import the can_lang dataset 
can_lang <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ttimbers/canlang/master/inst/extdata/can_lang.csv")

title: Making plots with ggplot2: Barplots and Scatterplots
Making plots with ggplot2: Barplots and Scatterplots
text:
Barplots with geom_col
Suppose we wanted to display this information in a barplot instead of in a table.

# start with just ggplot()
# blank canvas

ggplot(data=ten_lang)







# add data and aes()
# now we have axes but no data

ggplot(data=ten_lang, aes(x=language, y=mother_tongue))







# add data using geom_col


ggplot(data=ten_lang, aes(x=language, y=mother_tongue)) +
  geom_col()







#send in data without using new object

ten_lang |>
  ggplot(aes(x=language, y=mother_tongue)) +
  geom_col()







can_lang |>
  filter(category=="Aboriginal languages") |>
  arrange(desc(mother_tongue)) |>
  slice(1:10) |>
  ggplot(aes(x=language, y=mother_tongue)) +
  geom_col()








Is there any improvements we could make to this graph?

To better view text
Display the bars horizontally instead of vertically!

# switch axes to change orientation

ten_lang |>
  ggplot(aes(y=language, x=mother_tongue)) +
  geom_col()








This flips the x and y axes!


Labels, Colors, and Themes
We can alter the labels on our x and y axes.

# add axis labels and plot title

# using labs()
ten_lang |>
  ggplot(aes(y=language, x=mother_tongue)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x="Spoken as Mother Tongue",
       y="Language")







# using xlab() and ylab()

ten_lang |>
  ggplot(aes(y=language, x=mother_tongue)) +
  geom_col() +
  xlab("Spoken as Mother Tongue") +
  ylab("Language")














Tip



Barplots are good for displaying one categorical variable and one numeric variable. The number variable could be counts (as above) or they could be averages or totals or maximums or minimums (or many other things!)


We can change both the bar fill colors and outline colors displayed on the figure, by adding the color and fill arguments to our geom function.

# change bar colors using color= and fill=

ten_lang |>
  ggplot(aes(y=language, x=mother_tongue)) +
  geom_col(color="magenta", fill="limegreen") +
  xlab("Spoken as Mother Tongue") +
  ylab("Language")








We can further control the appearance of our figures with themes.

# play around with themes
ten_lang |>
  ggplot(aes(y=language, x=mother_tongue)) +
  geom_col(color="magenta", fill="limegreen") +
  xlab("Spoken as Mother Tongue") +
  ylab("Language") +
  theme_minimal()








You can find visualizations of all of the themes included in the ggplot2 package here. There are additional packages such as the ggthemes package that have even more themes. And if you are feeling really fancy, you can make your own custom theme (please don’t do this right now).
And then finally we can add a title to the figure using the ggtitle() function.

# add a title

ten_lang |>
  ggplot(aes(y=language, x=mother_tongue)) +
  geom_col(color="magenta", fill="limegreen") +
  xlab("Spoken as Mother Tongue") +
  ylab("Language") +
  ggtitle("Our Beautiful Plot") +
  theme_minimal()

title: Making plots with ggplot2: Barplots and Scatterplots
text:
Scatterplots with geom_point
The mtcars dataset was extracted from the 1974 Motor Trend US magazine, and comprises fuel consumption and 10 aspects of automobile design and performance for 32 automobiles (1973–74 models). It’s available inside the ggplot package which is already installed.

#load the data
data(mtcars)

#what is in the dataset???
#?mtcars







Tip



Scatterplots are good for displaying the relationship between two numerical variables.



Color and Shape

# what should we plot?

mtcars|>
  ggplot(aes(x=hp, y=mpg)) +
  geom_point()








We can change the shape of the points using the shape argument within our geom_point() function.

# change shape using pch (stands for plotting character)
# ?pch to get available point shapes

mtcars|>
  ggplot(aes(x=hp, y=mpg)) +
  geom_point(shape=8) +
  theme_minimal()








For reasons that are entirely unclear to me shapes in R are referred to as pch which stands for plotting character. They are called by number or in some cases name. The pch numbers and their corresponding shapes are shown below.

Likewise, we can change the color of our points using the color argument within our geom_point() function.

# change color outside of aes()
# call color by name

mtcars|>
  ggplot(aes(x=hp, y=mpg)) +
  geom_point(shape=8, color="purple") +
  theme_minimal()









# call color by hex code
mtcars|>
  ggplot(aes(x=hp, y=mpg)) +
  geom_point(shape=8, color="#7e1e9e") +
  theme_minimal()








In R you can call colors by name or by hex code. Named colors can be found here. A decent hex code color picker can be found here.


Mapping Data to Color

Quick update to the dataset

#code to update `mtcars` dataset so that `am` is treated as a factor rather than a continuous numeric variable
# used mutate and as.factor() to add column to existing dataset called am_factor

mtcars <- mtcars |>
  mutate(am_factor=as.factor(am))

This modifies the am column, which represents the transmission type of the car (0 = automatic, 1 = manual). The as.factor() function converts the am variable from a numeric type (0 or 1) into a categorical factor.

# what is a factor and how does it change the plotting?

#plot using normal am

mtcars |>
  ggplot(aes(x=hp, y=mpg, color=am)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_minimal()








Without turning am into a factor, it is plotted as a continuous variable with a color gradient for the variable.

#plot using am_factor

mtcars |>
  ggplot(aes(x=hp, y=mpg, color=am_factor)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_minimal()








If we use the factor version (am_factor), it plots as a discrete variable. Where a single color is assigned to each category.


Customizing Colors in Aesthetics
You can customize the colors that you use for both discrete/categorical variables and continuous variables using the scale_color_manual() and scale_color_gradient() functions, respectively.
First we are going to take a look at how to define colors for a discrete variable using the scale_color_manual() function and the am_factor variable that we created above which takes on the value of either 0 or 1.

# for discrete variables using scale_color_manual()

mtcars |>
  ggplot(aes(x=hp, y=mpg, color=am_factor)) +
  geom_point(size=3) +
  scale_color_manual(values=c("darkseagreen4","brown")) +
  theme_minimal()








We can also change the shape within the aes() function, and shape will be mapped to the two categories of am_factor in addition to color.

# change shape within aes()

mtcars |>
  ggplot(aes(x=hp, y=mpg, color=am_factor, shape=am_factor)) +
  geom_point(size=3) +
  scale_color_manual(values=c("darkseagreen4","brown")) +
  theme_minimal()








Now let’s take a look at how to do this for a continuous variable using the scale_color_gradient() function that you should already have access to with the packages that you have loaded.

# for continuous variables use scale_color_manual()

mtcars |>
  ggplot(aes(x=hp, y=mpg, color=qsec)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_gradient(low="pink", high="violetred4") +
  theme_minimal()








There are lots of ways to control the colors and palette and we will get into how to operate more of those controls in a few classes.






Tip




Use scale_color_manual() when assigning colors to categorical variables.
Use scale_color_gradient() when assigning colors to continuous variables.






Mapping Data to Shape
We can also map data to shape, just like we’ve done for color. Instead of using the color argument within the aes() function, we use the shape argument.

mtcars |>
  ggplot(aes(x=hp, y=mpg, shape=am_factor)) +
  geom_point(size=3) +
  theme_minimal()









Customizing Shapes in Aesthetics
If you want to control which shape is mapped to which variable, you can use the scale_shape_manual() function, which operates very similarly to the scale_color_manual() function.

# use the pch chart to find the numbers that correspond to different shapes

mtcars |>
  ggplot(aes(x=hp, y=mpg, shape=am_factor)) +
  geom_point(size=3) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(0, 2)) + 
  theme_minimal()








If we want to control which variable is given which shape (this can be especially useful when you have more than just two categories), we can adjust our call to the scale_shape_manual() function like this:

# use the pch chart to find the numbers that correspond to different shapes

mtcars |>
  ggplot(aes(x=hp, y=mpg, shape=am_factor)) +
  geom_point(size=3) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("0" = 2, "1" = 0)) +
  theme_minimal()








Hint: You can also control how colors are mapped to discrete variables using the same syntax inside of scale_color_manual().

title: Making plots with ggplot2: Barplots and Scatterplots
section: Global vs. Local Data and Aesthetics
text:
Global vs. Local Data and Aesthetics
Where you define your input data and aes() matters. Global aesthetic mappings apply to all geometries and can be defined when you initially call ggplot(). All the geometries added as layers will default to this mapping. Local aesthetic mappings add additional information or override the default mappings.
If we define our data mapping within the geom_point() function, additional geoms do not know anything about the mapping. We either have to define the mapping in each individual geom (locally):

#local variables
# geom_line() does not know about the data defined in geom_point()

# commented this figure out, because it is purposefully broken
# mtcars |>
#   ggplot() +
#   geom_point(aes(x=hp, y=mpg)) +
#   geom_line() + 
#   theme_minimal()

  ggplot() +
  geom_point(data=mtcars, aes(x=hp, y=mpg)) +
  geom_line(data=mtcars, aes(x=hp, y=mpg)) + 
  theme_minimal()








Or we need to define them at a higher level, inside the ggplot() function. This sets the mapping for all subsequent geoms, unless we explicitly say otherwise within the individual geoms:

# global variables
# if we define data and aesthetics in ggplot() every subsequent geom tht we call will know about them

mtcars |>
  ggplot(aes(x=hp, y=mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() + 
  theme_minimal()














Tip




If the thing you are trying to change (color, shape, size, etc.) depends on a variable, you should put in inside the aesthetics
If the thing you are trying to change (color, shape, size, etc.) should happen for all things, you should not put it inside the aesthetics.



We can map a variable to color within the aes() function locally so that the qsec variable is only mapped to color for geom_point() and not to geom_line().

#color = qsec as a local aesthetic
# set color gradient using scale_color_gradient()

mtcars |>
  ggplot(aes(x=hp, y=mpg)) +
  geom_line() + 
  geom_point(aes(color=qsec), size=3) +
  scale_color_gradient(low="blue4", high="thistle2") +
  theme_minimal()








We can overwrite global data mapping by setting color to a single value locally outside aes() if we want to override the data mapping for color and set it to single color instead.

# overwriting color = qsec as a global aesthetic with a local aesthetic in geom_point()

mtcars |>
  ggplot(mapping=aes(x=hp, y=mpg, color=qsec)) +
  geom_point(size=3, color="magenta") +
  scale_color_gradient(low="blue4", high="thistle2") +
  theme_minimal()

title: Making plots with ggplot2: Barplots and Scatterplots
text:
In-Class Excercise:

Plot 1
Create a scatterplot using geom_point() to explore the relationship between engine displacement (disp) and horsepower (hp) in the mtcars dataset. In addition to plotting these two numeric variables, map a third numeric variable of your choice to color. Apply a non-default continuous color scale using scale_color_gradient(), and include a clear title, axis labels, and a non-default theme. After creating your plot, write 2–3 sentences describing the pattern you observe between displacement and horsepower.


Plot 2
Now extend the story by investigating a different relationship in the dataset. Choose two numeric variables other than hp and disp that you think might help explain fuel efficiency or vehicle performance, and create a new scatterplot using geom_point(). Convert one relevant grouping variable (such as am, cyl, or gear) to a factor and map it to color. Apply a non-default discrete color scale using scale_color_manual(), and include a clear title, axis labels, and a theme. In 2–3 sentences, explain why you chose these variables and what you observe in the plot.

title: Data Science Sampler: Beyond Static Plots
text:
Setup
Here is where you may need to install some new packages:


Code
# Uncomment if needed
# install.packages(c("tidyverse", "leaflet", "plotly", "gganimate",
#                    "gapminder", "palmerpenguins"))

library(tidyverse)
library(leaflet) #new
library(plotly) #new
library(gganimate) #new
library(gapminder)
library(palmerpenguins)

title: Data Science Sampler: Beyond Static Plots
text:
Leaflet Interactive Maps
Let’s start with a basic map of earthquakes near New Zealand. We can set the earthquakes to size by magnitude. I messed around with the math a little to get a size ratio that I liked.


Code
data(quakes)

quakes |>
  slice_sample(n = 300) |>
  leaflet() |>
  addProviderTiles("Esri.OceanBasemap") |>
  addCircleMarkers(
    lng = ~long,
    lat = ~lat,
    # set circle marker to size by magnitude
    radius = ~mag^2/3,
    # make popup labels
    popup = ~paste0(
      "<strong>Magnitude:</strong> ", mag,
      "<br><strong>Depth:</strong> ", depth, " km"
    ),
    stroke = FALSE,
    fillOpacity = 0.6
  )






Color the points by magnitude and add a legend:


Code
pal <- colorNumeric(
  palette = "viridis",
  domain = quakes$mag
)

leaflet(quakes) |>
  addProviderTiles("Esri.OceanBasemap") |>
  addCircleMarkers(
    lng = ~long,
    lat = ~lat,
    radius = ~mag^2/3,
    color = ~pal(mag),
    stroke = FALSE,
    fillOpacity = 0.7
  ) |>
  addLegend(
    "bottomright",
    pal = pal,
    values = ~mag,
    title = "Magnitude"
  )






Now let’s start playing around with the basemaps. You can find all of the possibilities on this website:
https://leaflet-extras.github.io/leaflet-providers/preview/


Code
library(leaflet)
library(dplyr)

data(quakes)

small <- quakes |> filter(mag < 5)
large <- quakes |> filter(mag >= 5)

leaflet() |>
  # Basemaps
  addProviderTiles("Esri.WorldImagery", group = "Satellite") |>
  addProviderTiles("Esri.OceanBasemap", group = "Ocean") |>
  addProviderTiles("Stadia.StamenWatercolor", group = "Artsy") |>

  # Small earthquakes
  addCircleMarkers(
    data = small,
    lng = ~long, lat = ~lat,
    radius = 3,
    color = "blue",
    group = "Smaller quakes",
    stroke = FALSE,
    fillOpacity = 0.5
  ) |>

  # Large earthquakes
  addCircleMarkers(
    data = large,
    lng = ~long, lat = ~lat,
    radius = ~mag * 2,
    color = "red",
    group = "Larger quakes",
    stroke = TRUE,
    weight = 1
  ) |>

  # Layer control
  addLayersControl(
    baseGroups = c("Satellite", "Ocean", "Artsy"),
    overlayGroups = c("Smaller quakes", "Larger quakes"),
    options = layersControlOptions(collapsed = FALSE)
  )






Now with the EJI data. I strongly recommend that you don’t try to run this one.


Code
library(sf)
eji_data <- st_read("~/Dropbox/!Middlebury/Teaching/STAT 118/S2026/S2026_R_Proj/midterm/eji_sf.gpkg")

Code
eji_cali <- eji_data |>
  filter(STATE_NAME=="California") |>
  filter(!is.na(E_LIMENG), E_LIMENG <100)

pal <- colorNumeric(
  palette = "viridis",
  domain = eji_cali$E_LIMENG,
  na.color = "transparent"
)


eji_cali |>
leaflet() |>
  addTiles() |>
  addPolygons(
    fillColor = ~pal(E_LIMENG),
    fillOpacity = 0.7,
    color = "white",
    weight = 0.5,
    popup = ~paste0(
      "<strong>County:</strong> ", COUNTY,
      "<br><strong>Tract:</strong> ", GEOID,
      "<br><strong>Poverty %:</strong> ", E_LIMENG
    )
  ) |>

    "bottomright",
    pal = pal,
    values = ~E_LIMENG,
    title = "Unemployed",
    opacity = 0.7
  )

title: Data Science Sampler: Beyond Static Plots
text:
Plotly Interactive Plots
Plotly doesn’t change your analysis at all — it just changes how your results exist. It turns a static figure into something you could actually put on a website or share with someone to explore.
Let’s start simple. You make a plot in ggplot and then you feed it into plotly and it’s like magic.


Code
p <- ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, color = class,
                     text = paste("Model:", model))) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.7) +
  theme_minimal()

ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text")






Let’s add more information to the pop-up:


Code
p <- ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, color = class)) +
  geom_point(
    aes(text = paste(
      "Model:", model,
      "<br>Class:", class,
      "<br>Displacement:", displ,
      "<br>Highway MPG:", hwy
    )),
    size = 2,
    alpha = 0.7
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text")






Let’s try it with the gapminder data.


Code
p <-  gapminder |> 
  filter(year == 2007) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, color = continent)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(color="Continent") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_size(range = c(2, 10)) +
  ggtitle("Year: 2007") +
  theme_minimal()

ggplotly(p)






With facets:


Code
p <- ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy, color = class)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~drv) +
  theme_minimal()

ggplotly(p)






With a boxplot:


Code
p <- ggplot(mpg, aes(class, hwy, fill = class)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_minimal()

ggplotly(p)






This is my first time doing this with a boxplot, and now this is the only way I’m making a boxplot ever again!
Let’s do it with a line!


Code
economics <- ggplot2::economics

p <- ggplot(economics, aes(date, unemploy)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue") +
  theme_minimal()

ggplotly(p)






WITH A DENSITY PLOT!


Code
p <- ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = price, fill = cut)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5) +
  theme_minimal()

ggplotly(p)






This is AMAZING! Why am I only just learning this????

title: Data Science Sampler: Beyond Static Plots
text:
Animation
This animation shows the gapminder dataset through time, with GDP per capita on the x-axis and Life expectancy on the y-axis. The points are colored by continent and sized by population (on a log scale).


Code
p <- ggplot(
  gapminder,
  aes(
    x = gdpPercap,
    y = lifeExp,
    group = country,
    color = continent,
    size = pop
  )
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(1, 10)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Year: {frame_time}",
    x = "GDP per capita",
    y = "Life expectancy",
    color = "Continent",
    size = "Population"
  ) +
  transition_time(year)

animate(
  p,
  nframes = 60,
  fps = 4,
  width = 600,
  height = 400,
  renderer = gifski_renderer(),
  device = "ragg_png"
)


You may be able to tell by how many plots I made with the others and how few animations I have given you, that my heart isn’t really in animations. This single animation took about 50% of the time I spent making this. They can be a real pain. A good animation is absolute gold, but it is very hard to make a good animation.

title: Data Science Sampler: Beyond Static Plots
section: Spatial Data - but not people data
text:
Spatial Data - but not people data


Code
library(terra)
library(tidyterra)
library(cmocean)
library(ggthemes)
library(wesanderson)

volcano_df <- as.data.frame(volcano) |>
  mutate(y = row_number()) |>
  pivot_longer(-y, names_to = "x", values_to = "elevation") |>
  mutate(x = as.numeric(gsub("V", "", x)))

ggplot(volcano_df, aes(x, y, fill = elevation)) +
  geom_raster() + #not the way I choose to do this anymore, but workable for smaller data
  scale_fill_cmocean(name="thermal") +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_y_reverse() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Topographic-style raster map")









Here is some code from my Data Science Across Disciplines class this last January looking at instrumented seal data from the Southern Ocean.
First, some data prep. You are not expected to understand this part.


Code
seal_data <- read_csv("~/Dropbox/!middlebury/Teaching/DSAD 1230/DSAD_2026/R_code/MEOP_data_analysis/data/regional_data/par_seal_data.csv")
seal_data_surface <- seal_data |>
  filter(level==1)

raster_dir <- "/Users/caseysmith/Dropbox/!Middlebury/Teaching/DSAD 1230/DSAD_2025/R_code/Argo_vis_shiny_app"

PacSec_bathy <- rast(paste0(raster_dir, "/data/raster/PacSec_bathy.tif"))


#adjust seal data
seal_data_surface <- seal_data_surface |>
  mutate(lon_anti=case_when(lon<0 ~ lon+360,
                            lon>=0 ~lon))

seal_data_mod <- seal_data |>
  mutate(lon_anti=case_when(lon<0 ~ lon+360,
                            lon>=0 ~lon))

world <- map_data("world")


First a map with “raster” data.


Code
raster_dir <- "/Users/caseysmith/Dropbox/!Middlebury/Teaching/DSAD 1230/DSAD_2025/R_code/Argo_vis_shiny_app"

PacSec_bathy <- rast(paste0(raster_dir, "/data/raster/PacSec_bathy.tif")) 

ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data=PacSec_bathy) +
  scale_fill_cmocean(name="gray",
                     limits=c(-6000,0),
                     breaks=c(-6000,-5000,-4000,-3000,-2000,-1000,0),
                     labels=c("-6","-5","-4", "-3","-2","-1", "0")) +
  geom_polygon(data = world, 
               aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group),
               fill="white", color="white") +
   labs(fill="Depth (km)",
       x="Longitude", y="Latitude") +
  coord_sf(expand=FALSE, xlim = c(140,220), ylim=c(-70,-55) ) +
  ggtitle("Zoomed in on AAR/PAR, Bathymetry") +
  theme_tufte()









Code
ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data=PacSec_bathy) +
  scale_fill_cmocean(name="gray",
                     limits=c(-6000,0),
                     breaks=c(-6000,-5000,-4000,-3000,-2000,-1000,0),
                     labels=c("-6","-5","-4", "-3","-2","-1", "0")) +
  geom_polygon(data = world, 
               aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group),
               fill="white", color="white") +
  geom_point(data=seal_data_surface, 
             aes(x=lon_anti, y=lat, color=TEMP_ADJUSTED), 
             alpha=0.3, size=2) +
  scale_color_cmocean(name="thermal") +
  labs(fill="Depth (km)", color="Temp",
       x="Longitude", y="Latitude") +
  coord_sf(expand=FALSE, xlim = c(140,220), ylim=c(-70,-55) ) +
  ggtitle("Zoomed in on PAR, Bathymetry and Temperature") +
  theme_tufte()











Code
NPP_stack <- rast("~/Dropbox/!Research/Projects/PacAntRidge/data/NPP_raster_stack.nc")

invisible(capture.output({ #to suppress the #$^*@$ progress bar
NPP_stack[NPP_stack >100] = 100 #set max value
NPP_stack[NPP_stack <0] = NA #transform placeholder NA value (-99) to actual NA
}))

#my favorite palette from the wesanderson package
pal <- wes_palette("Zissou1", 100, type = "continuous")
ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data=NPP_stack[[15]]) + #index to show layer 15 only
  scale_fill_gradientn(colors=pal, limits=c(0,100)) +
  geom_spatraster_contour(data=PacSec_bathy, breaks=c(0,-3000)) + #contour to show margins of mid ocean ridge
  labs(fill="NPP",
       x = "Longitude",
       y = "Latitude") +
  xlim(130, 230) +
  ylim(-70, -55) +
  coord_sf(expand=FALSE) +
  theme_tufte() +
  ggtitle("NPP 2011-2012")









Code
#calculate the difference between the two years, by subtracting one from the other
diff_layer <- NPP_stack[[14]]-NPP_stack[[15]]

diff_layer[diff_layer > 75] = 75 #set max value
diff_layer[diff_layer < (-75)] = -75 #set min value


ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data=diff_layer) + 
  scale_fill_cmocean(name="balance", limits=c(-75,75)) + #change to diverging palette
  geom_spatraster_contour(data=PacSec_bathy, breaks=c(0,-3000)) +
  labs(fill="NPP",
       x = "Longitude",
       y = "Latitude") +
  xlim(130, 230) +
  ylim(-70, -55) +
  coord_sf(expand=FALSE) + #set this argument so that it doesn't add a border between the map and the axes
  theme_tufte() +
  ggtitle("NPP difference 2010-2011 minus 2011-2012")

text:
Resources

Canvas Site: Will be used for all assignments and contains the course schedule where absolutely everything will be linked
Course Schedule: This is probably the most important page for the entire course, everything will be linked here, it is available on the Canvas Site, under “Schedule” from the Homepage
Github Website: Completed notes will be rendered and posted to the site
Github Code Repository: Files used for homeowrk assignments and .qmd versions of class notes, as well as template files for class notes will be availble here



Syllabus

Assignments: See the Syllabus and Schedule for more details, but briefly, you will have 2 Homework Assignments per week, a Midterm Project, and a Final Project
Grade Allocation: Homework is 40% of your grade, Midterm Project is 25% and Final Project is 35%
Late Policy: See Syllabus for details



Thoughts on AI

Assignment prompts: You will be prompted at the end of your Homework Assignments to tell me whether you used AI, how you used it, and how you think it helped or hindered your learning
Thinking about what it gives you and what it takes away: I am not here to police your use of AI, but I do think it requires important consideration of how it impacts your learning (either positively or negatively)



Download Notes Template
These will always be linked on the Schedule (on the Canvas Site) before each class. You should download these at the beginning of class so that you will be better able to code along with me in class.


Directory structure
The directory structure outlined below is intended to prevent a number of headaches in how Quarto references files automatically. Please make sure that your files and folders are structured like this.
📁 STAT118/
   ├── class-notes.qmd
   ├── homework-01.qmd
   ├── homework-02.qmd
   ├── 📁 data/
   └── 📁 images/


R and Rstudio

What is the difference?
R is the engine and RStudio is the car.


What do the different windows do?
The Source window is where you will create and edit your Quarto documents, and write your code. This window should be in the top left pane.
The Console window is where the code is run. This window should be in the top right pane.
The Environment window will show you the objects and other things that you have created and defined in your code. this should be on the bottom left.
The window on the lower right should include Files, Plots, Packages, Help, and Viewer (it’s ok if there are additional tabs). This is where you can look for help documentation on the different functions available through R and additional R packages. This is also where figures and rendered files should pop up.



Settings

Rearrange panes
If your panes are not in the configuration outlined above, please change them using the instructions below.
Go to:
Tools → Global Options → Pane Layout


Change theme
If you want to change how your RStudio appears.
We decided that I could continue to use my dark theme. Yay!
Go to:
Tools → Global Options → Appearance


Change Downloads Permission
Please take a minute to change your downloads permissions for the browser that you use. This will make it easier for you to direct downloads to the correct folder and not have to go hunting for things that got sent to weird places.
Google Chrome:

Go to the three-dot menu (top-right corner) → Settings.
Scroll down and click Downloads.
Toggle on “Ask where to save each file before downloading.”

Firefox:

Click the three-line menu (top-right corner) → Settings.
In the General section, under Files and Applications, select: “Always ask you where to save files.”

Safari (Mac):

Go to Safari > Preferences > General.
Under File download location, select: “Ask for each download.”




Quarto

Source vs. Visual


Markdown Syntax

Bold and Italics
You make bold text by placing two * before and after the text you wish to bold: **make this text bold**
make this text bold
You make italics text by placing one * before and after the text you wish to appear in italics: *make this text italics*
make this text italics
You make bold and italics text by placing three * before and after the text you wish to appear in bold and italics: ***make this text bold and italics***
make this text bold and italics


Lists
To make a list put a - before each item on the list.
a list

-   one thing
-   second thing
-   third thing

The result will look like this:
a list

one thing
second thing
third thing

Always make sure to include an empty line before the first item on the list, otherwise it will not render properly.


Hyperlink
To add a hyperlink use this syntax:
[words here](link here)
The text should look like this:
[this is a link to the class website](https://cschine.github.io/my_class_website/courses/STAT118/)
The result will look like this:
this is a link to the class website


Images
To add an image, use this syntax:
![caption](image)
The text should look something like this:
![this is an image](images/NBP_midnight_sun.jpeg)
And the result will look like this:



this is an image





Using R in Quarto
R code chunks
Use the green +C buttom in the toolbar to add a code chunk
Create an object like this:

aardvark <- 17

yeti <- 23

You can do basic arithmetic with named objects using the standard operators:



Operator
Description




+
Addition


-
Subtraction


*
Multiplication


/
Division


^ or **
Exponentiation



Like this:

aardvark*yeti

[1] 391

aardvark/yeti

[1] 0.7391304

chalk <- aardvark*yeti

chalk

[1] 391


To comment code use the # at the beginning of the line and write a description of what the code should be doing, or a note to yourself, or whatever you want. Like this:

# multiply aardvark and yeti
aardvark*yeti

[1] 391

# divide aardvark by yeti
aardvark/yeti

[1] 0.7391304

# assign chalk a value of aardvark multiplied by yeti
chalk <- aardvark*yeti

# call chalk up
chalk

[1] 391




Render
Now it is time to Render your Quarto (.qmd) doc into a .html file (which is the format in which you will be submitting all of your assignments). To do this press the  Render button, which should be visible in the toolbar at the top of your Source Pane (the pane in which you are editing your Quarto document).
If your quarto doc does not render correctly, errors can be found in the Background Jobs tab in the Console Pane. This can be very useful and sometimes very confusing.



Assignments
Assignments will be linked on the Schedule on Canvas. If you are having any difficulty with your assignment please come to office hours sooner rather than later so that we can get things figured out.

title: Installing R and RStudio
text:
For this course, you will need to install both R and RStudio on your computer.

R is the programming language that runs your code.
RStudio is the program we will use to write and run R code.

Install R first, then install RStudio.

1. Install R
Go to the R Project download page.

Mac

Click Download R for macOS.
Download the appropriate installer for your Mac.
Open the downloaded .pkg file and follow the installation instructions.







Tip



If you are unsure which R version you need, click on the Apple in the upper lefthand corner of your desktop and select “About This Mac”, this will contain information both about the chip in your Mac (Intel or M) and the OS that you are running which will allow you to select the correct version of R.




Windows

Click Download R for Windows.
Click install R for the first time.
Click Download R-4.6.1 for Windows (the exact R version number may have changed).
Open the downloaded installer and accept the default installation options.




2. Install RStudio Desktop
Go to the RStudio Desktop download page.

Download the free version of RStudio Desktop for your operating system.
Open the installer.
Follow the installation instructions.



3. Make sure everything works
Open RStudio.



Credit: moderndive


If the installation was successful, you should see the RStudio interface with a Console pane containing some text about your version of R and a > prompt.
At the > prompt, type:

2 + 2

If R responds with:
[1] 4
you’re ready for class!
If you are stumped by 3. Don’t worry about it. If you didn’t get any errors during installation and can open the program ok, then you should be good to go.

title: Wrangling Basics
text:
A package is a bundle of tools that someone has written and shared to help you do specific kinds of work in R.
It usually contains:

Functions (the main thing you use)
Documentation (help files)
Sometimes example datasets

A package is like installing an “app” for R. Base R is what comes pre-installed and Packages are extra apps you download when you need new features



A function is a named command that does a specific job.
You give it inputs → it does something → it gives you an output.
It is like a button on a calculator. You press “mean” → it computes the mean.

Installing a package
You can install a package by selecting the packages tab your console pane where you have Files, Plots, Packages, etc. Then click on the install icon at the top left. Start typing in the package you want to install. It will give you some autofill options, you can type the whole thing in or select it from the autofill options. Then click on ‘Install’.
You can also run a simple line of code (which you can see in your R Console is what all the button clicking in the previous paragraph does).

# package name must be in quotes
#install.packages("tidyverse")

# after you have installed the package you do not need to install it again

You only run the install.packages() function for a given package one time and then once the package is installed you should not run this line of code again. Either comment it out or delete it. Now you have a copy of the package saved on your computer.

title: Wrangling Basics

distinct()
We can use distinct to get more information from the can_lang dataset. Such as the number of different language categories in the dataset.

# ?distinct() to look at the help documentation

distinct(select(can_lang, category))

  category

1 Aboriginal languages

3 Official languages

can_lang |>
  select(category) |>
  distinct()

1 Aboriginal languages                   
2 Non-Official & Non-Aboriginal languages
3 Official languages

title: Wrangling Basics
text:
filter()
We can use the filter function to extract rows from the data that match a certain condition or set of conditions.
We define the condition with a logical expression using the logical operators are given below:



Operator
Description




<
Less than


>
Greater than


<=
Less than or equal to


>=
Greater than or equal to


==
Equal to


!=
Not equal to


!x
Not x


x | y
x OR y


x & y
x AND y



For example, we may be interested in only looking at only the languages in this dataset that are Aboriginal languages.

# ?filter() for help documentation
# wants data and an expression that returns a logical value


# filter for only Aboriginal languages using pipe

can_lang |>
  filter(category == "Aboriginal languages")

# A tibble: 67 × 6
   category          language mother_tongue most_at_home most_at_work lang_known
   <chr>             <chr>            <dbl>        <dbl>        <dbl>      <dbl>

10 Aboriginal langu… Cayuga              45           10           10        125
# ℹ 57 more rows

# filter and then pipe into count() to get number of Aboriginal languages

can_lang |>
  filter(category == "Aboriginal languages") |>
  count()

# A tibble: 1 × 1
      n
  <int>
1    67


Oftentimes, we want to take our subset and give it a new name. This takes our subset and assigns it to a new dataset called aboriginal_lang.

# define new object with only aboriginal languages

aboriginal_lang <- can_lang |>
  filter(category == "Aboriginal languages")

Suppose we want a list of all the languages in Canada that are spoken by less than 100 people as their mother tongue.

# filter mother_tongue less than 100

can_lang |>
  filter(mother_tongue < 100)

arrange()
The arrange function allows us to order the rows of the data frame by the values of a particular column.

# filter for Aboriginal languages category then arrange (desc)

title: Wrangling Basics
text:
slice()
The slice function will allow us to pick only a subset of the rows based on their numeric order (1st through last).
For example, if I want a list of the 10 most commonly spoken aboriginal languages.

# filter for Aboriginal language, arrange descending, slice(1:10)
# arrange in descending order
# slice for rows 1 through 10

can_lang |>
  filter(category=="Aboriginal languages") |>
  arrange(desc(mother_tongue)) |>
  slice(1:10)

# A tibble: 10 × 6
   category          language mother_tongue most_at_home most_at_work lang_known

palmerpenguins dataset
Size measurements, clutch observations, and blood isotope ratios for adult foraging Adélie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo penguins observed on islands in the Palmer Archipelago near Palmer Station, Antarctica. Data were collected and made available by Dr. Kristen Gorman and the Palmer Station Long Term Ecological Research (LTER) Program.

#load data 
library(palmerpenguins) 
data(penguins)

drop_na()
drop_na() removes rows with missing data. If you use it with no additional arguments it will drop a row that contains an NA in any column.

# save as new object
# drop_na without pipe

penguins_mod <- drop_na(penguins)

# drop_na with pipe

penguins_mod <- penguins |>
  drop_na()

count()

title: Exploring and Summarizing Data
Exploring and Summarizing Data
text:
group_by()
Let’s say we were interested in the average bill length and bill depth of all penguin species in this dataset. We could repeat this for the other species (Gentoo and Chinstrap). This would be a fair amount of work AND the results would not end up in the same table.
OR we could use the group_by command!

# group_by species and then summarize bill length and bill depth (mean)


penguins |>
  group_by(species) |>
  drop_na(bill_length_mm) |>
  summarize(mean_bill_length=mean(bill_length_mm),
            mean_bill_depth=mean(bill_depth_mm))

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  species   mean_bill_length mean_bill_depth
  <fct>                <dbl>           <dbl>
1 Adelie                38.8            18.3
2 Chinstrap             48.8            18.4
3 Gentoo                47.5            15.0

penguins |>
  group_by(island) |>
  drop_na(bill_length_mm) |>
  summarize(mean_bill_length=mean(bill_length_mm),
            mean_bill_depth=mean(bill_depth_mm))

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  island    mean_bill_length mean_bill_depth
  <fct>                <dbl>           <dbl>
1 Biscoe                45.3            15.9
2 Dream                 44.2            18.3
3 Torgersen             39.0            18.4



Multiple Groups
Suppose we wish to have the average bill length and average bill depth broken down by sex AND species:

# group by species/sex and then summarize avg bill depth

penguins |>
  group_by(species, sex) |>
  drop_na() |>
  summarize(mean_bill_length=mean(bill_length_mm),
            mean_bill_depth=mean(bill_depth_mm))

# A tibble: 6 × 4
# Groups:   species [3]
  species   sex    mean_bill_length mean_bill_depth
  <fct>     <fct>             <dbl>           <dbl>
1 Adelie    female             37.3            17.6
2 Adelie    male               40.4            19.1
3 Chinstrap female             46.6            17.6
4 Chinstrap male               51.1            19.3
5 Gentoo    female             45.6            14.2
6 Gentoo    male               49.5            15.7

# do it again with NAs removed

We can also give the new calculated variables names of our choosing rather than letting R makes choices, because it does the wackiest stuff when left to its’ own devices.

title: Exploring and Summarizing Data
text:
mutate()
mutate() creates new columns that are functions of existing variables.

# first just create a new column that contains all 5s

penguins_mod <- penguins |>
  mutate(fives=5)

For example, let’s calculate create a new column which displays the body length weight in pounds (lbs) instead of grams. Recall: to convert from grams to pounds we need to multiply by 0.00220462.

# calculate body mass in lb from conversion factor (0.00220462 lb/g), create new column

penguins_mod <- penguins |>
  mutate(body_mass_lb=body_mass_g*0.00220462)


# then assign it to new object

This can be useful for unit conversions. It also be useful for making new calculations based on existing data, for example, the ratio of bill_length to bill_depth.

penguins_mod <- penguins_mod |>
  mutate(bill_ratio = bill_depth_mm/bill_length_mm)

title: Exploring and Summarizing Data
text:
case_when()
Case when can be used in combination with mutate to create a new column with a categorical variable conditional on the values in another column.
For example:

# penguins <- penguins |> 
#   mutate(penguin_length_cat = case_when(bill_length_mm > 50 ~ 'whoa! huge bill!', TRUE ~ '--' ))

# make a new column with a single letter for each penguin species

penguins_mod <- penguins_mod |>
  mutate(spp_abbr = case_when(species=="Adelie" ~ "A",
                              species=="Gentoo" ~ "G",
                              species == "Chinstrap" ~ "C"))


# make a new column with a body mass cutoff that labels penguins below the cutoff as "little" and the ones above it as "BIG"

penguins_mod <- penguins_mod |>
  mutate(size = case_when(body_mass_g >= 5000 ~ "BIG",
                          body_mass_g < 5000 ~ "little"))
